items.q: What does an inverted index actually store?

options.t: For each document, the list of terms it contains
options.why: That's the forward direction — what the raw document already is. The 'inverted' part is flipping it, so a query term leads straight to its documents.

options.t: For each term, a sorted list of the documents containing it, with frequencies and positions
options.why: Right. Term → posting list (doc IDs, sorted, plus per-doc frequency for ranking and word positions for phrases). One lookup per query term instead of scanning every document.

options.t: A B-tree over the concatenated text of all documents
options.why: B-trees are sorted by value from the first character, so they answer prefix questions only — that's exactly why LIKE '%term%' scans everything and why search needs a different structure.

options.t: A hash of each document's full text for deduplication
options.why: Content hashing helps dedupe (GitHub used it to shrink 115TB of code), but it can't answer 'which docs contain this word' — that's the posting list's job.

items.q: Posting lists are kept sorted by doc ID. What does that buy?

options.t: Results come back sorted by relevance automatically
options.why: Doc ID order has nothing to do with relevance — scoring happens separately. Sorting is for the matching step, not the ranking step.

options.t: Newer documents appear first in results
options.why: Doc IDs aren't a freshness ranking. Recency, if wanted, is a scoring feature in the rerank phase — not a property of posting order.

options.t: AND queries become cheap: two sorted lists intersect in one linear pass, and skip pointers let you leap blocks
options.why: Yes. Intersection of sorted lists is a two-finger merge, and skip data lets the rare term drive while whole compressed blocks of the common term's list are jumped over unread.

options.t: It makes the index smaller
options.why: Close to a real point — sorted IDs delta-encode well, which does compress — but the load-bearing reason is fast intersection. An unsorted list could be compressed too; it couldn't be intersected cheaply.

items.q: Why must a query pass through the same analyzer as the indexed documents?

options.t: The index stores analyzed terms — documents indexed 'flight' won't match a query for 'flights' unless the query stems the same way
options.why: Right. The analyzer is a contract between write and read. Mismatched analysis is the classic silent bug: zero errors, zero results.

options.t: For security, to sanitize user input
options.why: Sanitization is real but separate. The analyzer's job is linguistic normalization so query terms and index terms land in the same vocabulary.

options.t: To make queries case-sensitive
options.why: Backwards — analyzers usually lowercase both sides, making search case-insensitive. The point is doing the same thing on both sides, whatever that thing is.

options.t: It's an optimization; skipping it just makes queries slower
options.why: It's correctness, not speed. An unanalyzed query for 'Flights' against an index of stemmed lowercase terms doesn't run slowly — it finds nothing.

items.q: The textbook says drop stopwords ('the', 'to', 'a'). Why do modern engines keep them?

options.t: Disk got cheap, so why not
options.why: Cheap storage makes keeping them affordable, but that's the enabler, not the reason. There's a query class that breaks without them.

options.t: Phrase queries need them — 'the who' or 'to be or not to be' can't be matched from an index that threw those words away
options.why: Right. Phrases are verified from stored positions, and a phrase made of stopwords has nothing to verify against if they were dropped. Compression makes the cost bearable, and BM25's IDF already makes near-universal terms weigh almost nothing.

options.t: Stopwords carry the most relevance signal
options.why: The opposite — a term in every document discriminates nothing, which is exactly why dropping them was the old advice. They're kept for matching (phrases), not for scoring.

options.t: Removing them is too CPU-expensive at index time
options.why: Filtering a token stream against a small word list is nearly free. Cost was never the argument on either side.

items.q: BM25 improves on raw TF-IDF with two fixes. Which pair?

options.t: Synonym expansion and typo tolerance
options.why: Both real features, both living elsewhere — synonyms in query rewriting, typos in fuzzy matching. BM25 is purely a scoring formula over frequencies and lengths.

options.t: Term-frequency saturation and document-length normalization
options.why: Yes. The 50th occurrence of a term adds ~nothing (stuffing stops paying), and matches in a short doc outweigh the same matches buried in a long one. That's the whole trick, and it's been Lucene's default since 2016.

options.t: Click-through weighting and personalization
options.why: Behavioral signals belong to the rerank phase — BM25 can't see users at all. It's computed entirely from what's already in the posting lists.

options.t: Caching of scores and precomputed rankings
options.why: Those are systems optimizations, not scoring improvements. BM25 changed what the score IS, not how it's cached.

items.q: In Lucene's design, what is a segment?

options.t: A shard's replica on another machine
options.why: Replicas are whole-shard copies for availability. Segments live inside a single shard — they're how it organizes its own files.

options.t: A complete, immutable mini-index written once when the RAM buffer is refreshed, and never modified after
options.why: Right — term dictionary, postings, doc values, frozen at refresh time. Immutability is what allows aggressive compression, fearless caching, file-copy replication, and lock-free search.

options.t: The in-memory buffer where incoming documents wait
options.why: The buffer is the segment's larva — unsearchable RAM state. It becomes a segment at refresh, and that moment is when documents become findable.

options.t: A range of doc IDs assigned to one shard
options.why: That describes shard routing (and ours is by hash, not range). Segments are a storage-layer concept below sharding entirely.

items.q: Segments are immutable. So what happens when a document is deleted?

options.t: Its entries are removed from every posting list it appears in
options.why: That's the in-place update this whole design exists to avoid — hundreds of random writes into compressed sorted lists. Immutable means immutable.

options.t: The segment containing it is rewritten immediately without it
options.why: Rewriting a multi-gigabyte segment per delete would melt the disks. Rewriting does eventually remove it — but as a byproduct of a scheduled merge, not per delete.

options.t: It's marked dead in a per-segment tombstone bitmap; queries skip it, and a later merge physically drops it
options.why: Right. Deletes hide documents instantly and cheaply; reclaiming the bytes is deferred to background compaction. An update is this plus reindexing the new version into the buffer.

options.t: Deletes aren't supported; documents expire via TTL
options.why: Search indexes handle deletes constantly — every edited listing is a delete plus an insert. TTLs exist in some systems but aren't the mechanism.

items.q: 'Near-real-time search' means a new document becomes searchable…

options.t: At the next refresh, when the RAM buffer freezes into a segment — seconds after arrival, not instantly
options.why: Right. Visibility is per-refresh, not per-document. Add CDC pipeline lag upstream and the honest promise is 'searchable within a few seconds' — say it before the interviewer asks.

options.t: The moment the indexer acknowledges it
options.why: Acknowledged means buffered (and durable upstream in Kafka), not searchable. The buffer is invisible to queries until refresh freezes it.

options.t: After the next background merge completes
options.why: Merges compact already-searchable segments — they affect efficiency, not visibility. Waiting for merges would mean minutes-to-hours of delay.

options.t: Within milliseconds, like a database read-after-write
options.why: That's the promise this architecture deliberately doesn't make. Per-document visibility would mean per-document segments — the design trades instant visibility for sequential-write indexing.

items.q: How do documents get into the search index in this design?

options.t: The application writes to the database and the index in the same request
options.why: Dual-write — no transaction spans both systems, so a crash between the writes leaves them silently disagreeing forever. Chapter 1.14 buried this pattern.

options.t: CDC tails the database's replication log, publishes changes to Kafka, and indexers consume them
options.why: Right. The DB's own commit log feeds the index, so nothing committed is missed, indexers can replay after crashes, bursts are absorbed by the queue, and consumer lag is your freshness metric for free.

options.t: A nightly batch job re-indexes changed rows
options.why: That's how it worked when 'searchable tomorrow' was acceptable. Our requirement is seconds, which needs a continuous stream, not a cron.

options.t: Sellers' clients POST documents directly to the search API
options.why: The index would become a second source of truth drifting from the catalog DB. There is deliberately no write API — search is derived data.

items.q: A teammate proposes sharding the index by term: machine 1 holds terms A–C, machine 2 holds D–F… 'Single-term queries touch one machine!' What kills it?

options.t: Multi-term queries: the posting lists for 'cheap' and 'goa' live on different machines, so intersecting them means shipping millions of doc IDs across the network per query — plus the machine holding 'iphone' becomes a hot partition
options.why: Both barrels. The expensive operation (intersection) becomes a network operation, and Zipf-skewed term popularity bakes in a celebrity problem. Doc sharding keeps every intersection local; only tiny top-K lists travel.

options.t: The alphabet doesn't split evenly across machines
options.why: Uneven letter distribution is trivially fixable by hashing terms. The real killers are cross-shard intersection and hot terms — problems no rebalancing fixes.

options.t: It can't support ranking
options.why: Scoring could be bolted on (painfully). The design dies earlier — at the matching step, where posting lists must cross the network to be intersected.

options.t: Terms change too often to assign stably
options.why: The vocabulary is actually fairly stable, and hashing handles new terms fine. Assignment isn't the issue; what queries make the shards DO to each other is.

items.q: A seller edits a listing title, searches 3 seconds later, and sees the old title. Support files a bug. Your diagnosis?

options.t: The CDC pipeline has crashed — page the on-call
options.why: Check indexing lag before paging anyone — 3 seconds is within the normal budget (CDC hop plus refresh interval). Lag alarms exist so you know the difference between 'working as designed' and 'broken'.

options.t: Working as designed: commit → CDC → Kafka → indexer → next refresh adds up to a few seconds, inside the stated freshness SLO — though the seller's own view could be fixed with read-your-writes from the source DB
options.why: Right. Walk the pipeline calmly with numbers, then note the product refinement: the author seeing their own edit is a read-your-own-writes problem, servable by ID from the database without touching search freshness at all.

options.t: The refresh interval is misconfigured and must be lowered to 100ms
options.why: That 'fix' births twenty tiny segments a second and collapses query latency. The pipeline is behaving; the requirement needs interrogating, not the knob cranking.

options.t: A real bug: the delete-and-reinsert must have resurrected the old version
options.why: Version-conflict resurrection is a real failure mode (which document versioning prevents), but it produces a stale doc that persists — not one that's simply 3 seconds behind. Occam says pipeline latency.

items.q: Query p50 is flat, but p99 spikes for a minute or two every ten-ish minutes on one shard. First suspect?

options.t: A slow network switch
options.why: Possible, but network trouble rarely arrives on a tidy periodic schedule confined to one shard. The rhythm is the clue — something scheduled is running.

options.t: Hot celebrity documents
options.why: A hot doc would push p50 too, and wouldn't oscillate on a timer. Skewed traffic looks sustained, not periodic.

options.t: A background segment merge saturating disk I/O and evicting the page cache queries depend on
options.why: The classic signature: merges are periodic, heavy, and local to a shard — they steal disk bandwidth and flush the cache, so the tail suffers while the median (served from remaining cache) holds. Check merge activity against the latency timeline before blaming anything else.

options.t: Garbage collection pauses
options.why: A reasonable second suspect — GC also causes periodic tail pain. But in a search node the first look goes to merge I/O, because this system's defining tension is indexing I/O versus query cache, and merge schedules match the period.

items.q: The merchandising team updates the synonym list ('sofa'='couch'='settee') most weeks. Index-time or query-time expansion?

options.t: Query time: rewrite queries to (sofa OR couch OR settee) — list changes take effect instantly, at a small per-query cost
options.why: Right. Index-time expansion bakes the list into every posting — each weekly edit would demand a full reindex of 200M docs. Paying a slightly fatter query beats paying a reindex per synonym tweak.

options.t: Index time: queries stay fast, and reindexing weekly is fine
options.why: A defensible trade in principle, but run the numbers: a full 200M-doc reindex every week as routine overhead, forever, to save an OR-clause per query. The cost-benefit points firmly the other way for a volatile list.

options.t: Both, for safety
options.why: Doing it twice double-expands queries into mush and still inherits index-time's reindex-on-change problem. Pick the one that matches how often the list changes.

options.t: Neither — synonyms belong in the ML rerank phase
options.why: The reranker only sees the top-1000 retrieved. If 'couch' docs were never retrieved for a 'sofa' query, no reranker can rescue them — synonym expansion must happen at retrieval.

items.q: BM25 uses shard-local IDF in your design. When would that visibly mis-rank results?

options.t: Always — global and local statistics never agree
options.why: They agree to within noise when each shard is a big random sample. The senior skill here is knowing when an approximation is safe, not rejecting all approximations.

options.t: When shards are small or non-randomly filled — say, per-tenant or per-category shards — so 'how rare is this term' differs by shard and scores stop being comparable at merge time
options.why: Right. With 20M randomly-routed docs per shard, local frequencies mirror global ones and the drift is invisible. Break the random-sample property and cross-shard score comparison wobbles — the fix is periodic global-stats sync or a two-pass query.

options.t: During bulk imports
options.why: Imports strain freshness and merge I/O, not IDF math — document frequencies shift slowly even during heavy writes. Wrong failure mode for this knob.

options.t: Whenever two shards return the same document
options.why: They can't — each doc is hashed to exactly one shard. Duplicate results would be a routing bug, unrelated to scoring statistics.

items.q: The results page shows 'Brand: Sony (812), Bose (340)…' computed over all matching docs. Which structure serves this?

options.t: The inverted index, walked in reverse
options.why: The inverted index answers term → docs. Facets need the opposite — doc → field value, for thousands of matched docs — and walking postings backwards to get it would be absurdly slow.

options.t: A separate Redis counter per brand
options.why: Pre-counted totals can't answer facet counts, because the counts are per-query — Sony's count within THIS search's matches. It has to be computed over the match set at query time.

options.t: Doc values: a columnar doc-ID → field-value array kept alongside the index, scanned for the matching docs at query time
options.why: Right — a column store bolted onto the text index. Filters, facet counting, sort-by-price, and rerank feature lookups all read this structure; it's built at the same segment-write time as everything else.

options.t: The source database, queried per search
options.why: Re-checking 400K matches against Postgres per search recreates the load the index exists to absorb. The index carries its own columnar sidecar precisely so it never has to phone home per query.

items.q: Where do click-through rate, seller reputation, and (later) an ML relevance model plug into this architecture?

options.t: Into BM25's formula as extra weights
options.why: BM25 runs over every matching doc — millions — so it must stay cheap, computable straight from postings. Stuffing expensive features into phase one prices you out of your latency budget.

options.t: Phase two: rerank the ~1000 BM25-retrieved candidates with the expensive signals
options.why: Right — retrieve-then-rerank. Cheap scorer earns a small candidate set; expensive scorer spends its budget only there. This is the socket ML (and vector similarity, chapter 3.24) plugs into without touching the index below.

options.t: At index time, baked into each document's stored score
options.why: Precomputed static quality scores exist, but click-through and personalization change per user and per hour — baking them into immutable segments means a reindex per update. Dynamic signals belong at query time.

options.t: In the client, re-sorting the returned page
options.why: The client only sees 20 results — reordering them can't surface a great doc ranked 500th by BM25. Reranking must happen where the top-1000 still exists: the coordinator.

items.q: Dashboard: segment count per shard has climbed steadily for six hours. Query latency is still normal. What is this telling you?

options.t: Nothing — segment count naturally grows forever
options.why: It naturally oscillates: refreshes add segments, merges remove them. Sustained growth means the equilibrium is broken — one side of that loop is losing.

options.t: Merges are falling behind indexing; every query pays per-segment overhead, so latency will follow within hours — investigate merge throughput now, while it's cheap
options.why: Right — this is a leading indicator, the kind worth alarming on. Cause could be an import burst, throttled merge I/O, or a sick disk. Waiting for the p99 alarm means fixing it during the fire instead of before it.

options.t: Disk is filling up; add storage
options.why: More segments isn't meaningfully more bytes — the same docs are just spread across more files. The cost is per-query work and a growing compaction debt, not capacity.

options.t: The refresh interval is too long
options.why: Backwards — a LONGER refresh would mean fewer, larger segments. If anything, stretching refresh during heavy indexing is a mitigation, not the cause.

items.q: All copies of shard 4 are down. Marketplace search queries arrive. Your committed behavior?

options.t: Serve results from the nine healthy shards, mark the response partial, log and alarm on the partial-result rate
options.why: Right for THIS product: 90% of the catalog beats an error page in a purchase funnel. The flag matters — silent degradation is how you lose a week to 'search seems worse lately'. And the commit flips for compliance search, where incomplete-but-confident answers are the worst outcome.

options.t: Fail all queries until shard 4 recovers
options.why: This turns a 10% recall loss into a 100% outage of a revenue-critical page. Fail-closed is the right commit for legal discovery — for commerce it's self-harm.

options.t: Retry the query until shard 4 comes back
options.why: Retrying against a dead shard adds latency and load and returns nothing — with every copy down there's nowhere for the retry to land. Answer with what you have, flagged.

options.t: Serve the nine shards' results without telling anyone — users won't notice
options.why: Users mostly won't; your relevance metrics and support queue will, mysteriously. Degrade openly: flag the response, count it, alarm on it. The difference between graceful degradation and silent data loss is the flag.

items.q: Thirty seconds into 'design search', you name where you'll spend your depth. The strongest crux call?

options.t: "The hard part is keeping the index fresh: an inverted index is a frozen structure — sorted, compressed posting lists — and I have to absorb thousands of updates a second into it while serving queries. That's segments, refreshes, and merges, and I'll spend my main dive there."
options.why: That's the fire. The reconciliation of 'immutable by design' with 'seconds-fresh by requirement' is what this question uniquely probes — matching, ranking, and fan-out are important but far more routine. Naming the tension in one sentence is the senior open.

options.t: "The hard part is scale — 200M documents is a lot of data."
options.why: Run the numbers: ~300GB of index. Small data. Calling volume the crux signals the estimation didn't drive the thinking — the interesting pressures are QPS fan-out and update absorption, not bytes.

options.t: "The hard part is choosing between Elasticsearch and OpenSearch."
options.why: A procurement decision, not an engineering one — they're forks of the same design. The interviewer wants what's inside the box, not which sticker is on it.

options.t: "The hard part is the ranking ML model."
options.why: Ranking ML matters in real products, but in this interview it slots neatly into the rerank phase — an extension point, not a tension. The structural difficulty lives in the index-update machinery.

items.q: PM demands: 'When a seller hits save, search must reflect it in under 100ms.' The senior response?

options.t: Set the refresh interval to 50ms and ship it
options.why: Twenty micro-segments per second per shard: segment counts explode, per-query overhead multiplies, merges drown. This 'fix' trades a freshness complaint for a site-wide latency incident.

options.t: Interrogate the requirement first: 'visible to whom?' The seller seeing their own edit is read-your-own-writes — serve it by ID from the source DB instantly — while everyone else keeps seconds-level refresh; commit to that split and say what true 100ms-for-all would cost
options.why: Wait — this IS the senior answer. If you picked it, re-read the option marked correct; they should match.

options.t: Interrogate the requirement: the seller seeing their own edit is read-your-own-writes, servable by ID from the source database with no search-index change; global 100ms visibility is a different, far more expensive ask — quote its cost separately and commit to the split
options.why: Right. Most 'instant search' demands dissolve into read-your-writes for the author plus normal refresh for the world. Splitting the requirement, serving the real need cheaply, and pricing the expensive interpretation honestly — that's the E5 pattern.

options.t: Explain that search engines can't do this and the requirement must be dropped
options.why: Half-true and unhelpful — engines do offer real-time-get by ID, and the underlying user need is usually fully servable. 'No' without decomposing the ask reads as inflexibility, not judgment.

items.q: The interviewer 10x's the corpus: 2 billion docs, same 2K QPS. What actually degrades first, and why?

options.t: Storage costs — 10x the disk
options.why: Disk is the cheapest thing in the room; ~3TB of index across a fleet is a rounding error. If your first concern at 10x is bytes, the estimation isn't driving the answer.

options.t: Nothing, if you add replicas
options.why: Replicas multiply read capacity for the SAME data. This axis grows the data: replicas of 10 overloaded shards don't help — you need ~100 shards, and that's where the pain starts.

options.t: Tail latency: ~100 shards means every query's p99 is the max over 100 machines, so it worsens by pure statistics even with all shards healthy — plus 10x merge I/O grinding against query cache on every node
options.why: Right. Fan-out width is the hidden cost of doc sharding, and max-over-N is brutal arithmetic: more shards, worse tails, no one at fault. Counters: hedged requests, partitioning so queries touch fewer shards, and splitting the indexing tier with segment-file replication.

options.t: BM25 stops working at that document count
options.why: BM25 is per-shard local math over posting statistics — it's indifferent to global corpus size. If anything, bigger random shards make its IDF approximation better.

items.q: Candidate A: 'I'd use Elasticsearch — it handles sharding and replication for us.' Candidate B says the same, then walks through segments and refresh honesty, CDC feeding a derived index, doc-sharded fan-out, and where merges will hurt. Both 'used Elasticsearch.' Why does only B pass at senior?

options.t: B memorized more Elasticsearch trivia
options.why: Nothing B said is trivia — segments, fan-out, and derived-store discipline are the design itself. Trivia would be flag names and version numbers; B showed mechanisms and their failure modes.

options.t: The tool's name is not a design: B demonstrated ownership of what's inside — the freshness promise, the update machinery, the failure modes they'd be paged for — which is what the question was probing through the tool
options.why: Right. 'Use X' outsources the thinking to a box the candidate can't open; every senior probe ('why is the edit not searchable?', 'why did p99 spike?') lands inside that box. B can answer them; A's design ends where the questions begin.

options.t: A should have built search from scratch instead of using a product
options.why: Using Lucene-based infrastructure is the correct engineering call — nobody wants you writing a posting-list codec in an interview. The bar isn't avoiding the tool; it's being able to open its lid.

options.t: B took longer, and interviews reward thoroughness
options.why: Time spent isn't the metric — plenty of candidates fill 45 minutes without depth. B's minutes carried mechanism, commitment, and failure-awareness; that content, not the duration, is the difference.

items.q: Relevance is suffering because the stemmer is too aggressive; you need a different analyzer. The index holds 200M live documents. Your move?

options.t: Change the analyzer config and restart the cluster
options.why: The old analysis is physically baked into every posting of every segment — a config flip makes new writes and all queries disagree with 200M already-indexed docs. Relevance wouldn't degrade; it would shatter.

options.t: Write a script that re-analyzes documents in place, segment by segment
options.why: Segments are immutable — 'in place' isn't an operation this storage layer has. Any rewrite path ends up building new segments anyway, which is just a reindex without the safety rails.

options.t: Build a new index version with the new analyzer, bulk-load from a DB snapshot, let CDC catch it up, compare result quality side by side, then flip the alias — old index kept warm for rollback
options.why: Right — reindex-from-source, the expand-and-contract migration of chapter 2.11 in search costume. It exists precisely because the index is derived data; teams that run it routinely treat analyzer changes as a Tuesday, not an incident.

options.t: Only apply the new analyzer to documents indexed from now on
options.why: Now the corpus is split-brained: the same query stems one way against new docs and another against old ones, and which results you get depends on indexing date. A quiet, permanent relevance bug — worse than the stemmer you started with.

items.q: Every big catalog import tanks query p99 for the duration. The business needs both imports and fast search. Your committed plan, short-term to long-term?

options.t: Now: throttle merge I/O, stretch the refresh interval during imports, schedule bulk loads off-peak, and let replicas favor queries. At the next order of magnitude: split indexing onto its own tier and replicate by copying finished segment files to searchers
options.why: Right — this is the 'two workloads fight' tension managed at increasing cost. The knobs buy time cheaply; the tier split (the design Amazon's Lucene-based product search uses) removes the fight structurally, because immutable segments make replication a file copy.

options.t: Add more CPU to the index nodes
options.why: The contention is disk I/O and page cache, not cycles — merges evict the cache queries live on. Bigger boxes dilute the pain without addressing the mechanism, and the next import proves it.

options.t: Pause all indexing during business hours
options.why: This sacrifices the freshness SLO on the altar of latency — sellers' edits invisible all day. A commitment that deletes a requirement isn't a trade-off, it's a surrender.

options.t: Route queries to the replica with the least indexing load, and call it done
options.why: A real knob (and part of the right answer) presented as the whole answer. Replicas doing their own indexing still merge and still evict cache — without throttling and eventually a tier split, the fight follows you to every copy.

items.q: Same architecture, new customer: a legal e-discovery product where lawyers must certify that a search returned ALL responsive documents. Which single committed behavior must flip from the marketplace design?

options.t: Shard-loss handling: partial results must become a loud failure — an incomplete answer presented as complete is the worst possible outcome for this product, so fail closed and say why
options.why: Right. For commerce, 90% recall flagged is graceful degradation; for a court-certified search it's a professional catastrophe wearing a success status code. Same machine, opposite commit — knowing that the product dictates the failure semantics IS the senior signal this question hunts.

options.t: Switch ranking from BM25 to exact boolean matching
options.why: E-discovery does lean on boolean queries, but ranking choice isn't the life-or-death flip — you can rank however you like as long as the MATCH SET is complete and honest. Completeness semantics outrank scoring choices here.

options.t: Drop the refresh interval to zero for instant indexing
options.why: Discovery corpora are mostly static once ingested — freshness pressure goes DOWN in this product, not up. The knob that must move is what happens when part of the index can't answer.

options.t: Move the index into the source-of-truth database so nothing is derived
options.why: The derived-index architecture is fine — desirable, even, since reindex-from-source gives you a provable rebuild story. What changes is the promise made when a shard is missing, not where the index lives.
